topic.title: Resolving forces into components
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 2 is one hour and fifty marks over six questions, sat every Summer. Resolving is a step inside a longer forces question rather than a question of its own, and it appears in two or three of the six questions every year, usually for 2 or 3 marks a part. The reports name the sine and cosine mix-up in almost every series, which makes these the marks most often thrown away by candidates who understand the mechanics.
mustMemorise: Component along a line = F cos of the angle between the force and that line
Component at right angles to it = F sin of the same angle
On a slope of angle a: mg sin a down the slope, mg cos a into it
Turn a mass into a weight with g = 10 before resolving
A component that points the other way is subtracted
notOnThisSpec: Resolving in two directions that are not at right angles to each other
The coefficient of friction and F = μR: a frictional force is given, as a number or as so many newtons per kilogram
g = 9.8 m/s²: this unit takes g = 10 m/s², as the front page of every FM2 paper states

mustBeAbleTo: Draw the right-angled triangle that splits a force into two components
Write the component along a line as F cos of the angle between the force and that line
Write the component at right angles to it as F sin of the same angle
Turn a mass into a weight before resolving it
Resolve the weight of a body on a slope into mg sin of the slope's angle down it and mg cos into it
Read whether an angle is given to the horizontal, to the vertical or to the plane, and use the right one
Give a component a sign, and subtract one that points the other way
Round a component to 2 decimal places when the question says so
sheet.howExamined: Unit 2, one hour, fifty marks, six questions, calculator allowed, formula sheet on page 2. Resolving sits inside a longer forces question and carries 2 or 3 marks a part: Summer 2025 Q6(ii) asked for the normal reaction on a slope for 2, Summer 2023 Q3(i) and (ii) for 2 each, and Summer 2024 Q3(i) and (ii) for 3 each where two angled forces had to be resolved before an equation could be written. The scheme gives MW for a correct resolved component and W for the value, with follow-through into the parts that use it.
traps: Sine and cosine interchanged, the error the reports name year after year (Summer 2024 Q3, Summer 2025 Q6(ii), Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii))
An angle measured from the wrong line, so a force given at an angle to the vertical or to the plane is resolved as though it were given to the horizontal (Summer 2024 Q3)
A force left unresolved, with its whole magnitude put into the working (Summer 2024 Q3)
The magnitude of a force and its angle mixed up when resolving (Summer 2024 Q3)
g left out, so the mass is resolved instead of the weight (Summer 2019 Q3(ii))
A component that acts the other way added instead of subtracted (Summer 2022 Q3(b)(ii), Summer 2024 Q3)

workedExamples.stem:
A sledge is pulled along level ground by a rope. The pull along the rope is $42$ N and the rope makes an angle of $28°$ with the ground.

Calculate the component of the pull
(i) parallel to the ground,
(ii) at right angles to the ground.

Round each answer to 2 decimal places.

figure.alt: A force of 42 N drawn as an arrow at 28 degrees above a horizontal line. Dashed lines complete a right-angled triangle: the side along the floor is labelled 42 cos 28 degrees and the side at right angles to it is labelled 42 sin 28 degrees.

steps.working: The pull, the ground and the dashed vertical make a right-angled triangle with the $28°$ angle at the sledge.
steps.decision: Draw the triangle before choosing a ratio: the angle has to be marked between the force and the line you are resolving along.

options: Because the ratio depends on which side of the angle the direction lies
Because the triangle gives the size of the force
Because the angle must always be measured from the horizontal
whyMenu.explain: The force is known already. What the triangle settles is which of its two shorter sides you want, and that is what fixes sine or cosine.

steps.decision: The ground is the side beside the angle, so this component takes the cosine.

steps.working: At right angles to the ground: $42\sin 28° = 19.72$ N.
steps.decision: The upward direction is opposite the angle, so this one takes the sine.

steps.working: Check: the size of the pull is $\sqrt{37.08^2 + 19.72^2} = 42.00$ N.
steps.decision: The two components are the legs of a right-angled triangle whose longest side is the force, so Pythagoras is a free check.

figure.alt: A box of mass 9 kg on a slope inclined at 24 degrees. A solid arrow from the box points straight down and is labelled 90 N. Two dashed arrows split it: one down the slope labelled 90 sin 24 degrees and one into the slope labelled 90 cos 24 degrees.

steps.decision: Turn the mass into a force first: a component of a mass means nothing, and g = 10 on this paper.

steps.working: The angle between the weight and the line into the slope is the slope's own angle: $\theta = 24°$.
steps.decision: The two right angles in the picture force it: tilt the surface by 24° and the normal tilts by 24° as well.
Down the slope is opposite that angle, so it takes the sine.
Into the slope sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine. It is the larger of the two for any slope under 45°.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: in a right-angled triangle, which ratio connects the angle to the side next to it and the longest side?

options.feedback: Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, so it reaches the side beside the angle.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so it reaches the side across from the angle.
Tangent connects the two shorter sides and leaves the longest one out.
That relates the three sides but uses no angle at all.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: work out $30\cos 60°$.

options.feedback: $\cos 60° = 0.5$, so the answer is half of 30.
That leaves the cosine out altogether.
That is $30\sin 60°$.
That is the cosine on its own, without the 30.

items.stem: From an earlier topic: taking $g = 10$ m/s², what is the weight of a body of mass $14$ kg?

options.feedback: That is the mass with newtons written after it.
That divides by $g$ instead of multiplying.
That uses $g = 9.8$, which this unit does not.

items.stem: A force $F$ acts at an angle $\theta$ to a straight line. Which expression gives its component along that line?

options.feedback: The line is the side beside the angle, so the cosine gives the part along it.
That is the component at right angles to the line, opposite the angle.
Tangent compares the two components with each other, not either of them with the force.
A component is never bigger than the force it came from, so it is multiplied, not divided.

items.stem: A body of weight $W$ rests on a slope inclined at $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Which expression gives the component of $W$ at right angles to the slope?

options.feedback: The slope's angle sits between the weight and the line into the surface, so that component takes the cosine.
That is the component down the slope.
The whole weight only presses into the surface when the surface is horizontal.
Tangent would make the component larger than the weight once the slope passes 45°.

items.skill: An angle given to the vertical
items.stem: A force of $24$ N acts at $40°$ to the vertical. Which expression gives its horizontal component?

options.feedback: The angle is measured from the vertical, so the horizontal direction is the one opposite it.
That would be right if the $40°$ were measured from the horizontal. Read which line the angle is given to.
That takes the $50°$ from the horizontal but then the sine of it, which gives the vertical part, the same as $24\cos 40°$. The horizontal part is $24\sin 40°$.
Tangent compares the two components and cannot give either from the force.

items.stem: A rope pulls a box up a slope. The rope is at $25°$ to the slope and the slope is at $15°$ to the horizontal. Which angle is used to resolve the pull along the slope?

options.feedback: The angle between the rope and the slope is the one that belongs in the cosine.
That is the slope's own tilt, which the weight uses, not the rope.
That is the rope's angle to the horizontal, which would resolve along the ground instead.
Subtracting the two angles measures nothing on the diagram.

items.skill: Combining components that face each other
items.stem: One pull gives a component of $30$ N to the right and another gives $12$ N to the left. What is the total component to the right?

options.feedback: Opposite directions subtract, so $30 - 12 = 18$ N to the right.
Adding treats the second pull as helping the first, when it works against it.
Components are added and subtracted, never multiplied.
That leaves the first component out of the total altogether.

context.setting: A crate resting on a ramp

parts.stem:
A crate of mass $14$ kg rests on a ramp inclined at $18°$ to the horizontal.

Calculate the component of the weight of the crate acting down the ramp. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Turn the mass into a weight first.
Down the slope is opposite the slope's angle.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 14 \times 10 = 140$ N, so the component down the ramp is $140\sin 18° = 43.26$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $140\cos 18°$, the component pressing into the ramp. Down the ramp is opposite the ramp's angle, so it takes the sine.
That resolves the mass instead of the weight. Multiply by $g$ first: the weight is $140$ N.

parts.stem:
Calculate the component of the weight acting at right angles to the ramp. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Into the slope sits beside the slope's angle.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $140\sin 18°$, the component down the ramp. Into the ramp sits beside the ramp's angle, so it takes the cosine.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 14 * 10; down = W * sin(18 deg); into = W * cos(18 deg)

context.setting: A rope at an angle to a slope

parts.stem:
A rope pulls a box up a slope. The slope is inclined at $20°$ to the horizontal and the rope is inclined at $35°$ to the slope. The pull along the rope is $50$ N.

Calculate the component of the pull acting along the slope. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Which angle lies between the rope and the slope?
parts.workedSolution: Component along the slope $= 50\cos 35° = 40.96$ N. The slope's own tilt of $20°$ belongs to the weight, not to the rope.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $50\sin 35°$, the component at right angles. The one along the line sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.
That treats the $35°$ as the rope's angle to the horizontal and takes the slope's $20°$ off it. The $35°$ is already measured from the slope, so use it as it is.

parts.stem:
A ring at $O$ is pulled by a force of $34$ N acting horizontally to the right, and by a force of $20$ N acting at $60°$ above the horizontal, to the left.

Calculate the total component of the two forces to the right.

Answer ________ N
hints: Resolve the slanted pull first.
Which of the two horizontal parts faces the other way?
parts.workedSolution: $20\cos 60° = 10$ N to the left, so the total to the right is $34 - 10 = 24$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The resolved component is right, which earns the method mark (M), but the second pull acts to the left, so it is taken away rather than added.
That takes the whole $20$ N away. Only its horizontal part, $20\cos 60°$, acts along the line you are working in.

context.setting: A pull and a resistance on a trolley

parts.stem:
A trolley is pulled forwards along level ground by a force of $38$ N acting at $25°$ to the ground. A resistance of $15$ N acts along the ground, against the motion.

Calculate the total force on the trolley along the ground, in the direction it is moving. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Only the part of the pull along the ground drives the trolley.
The resistance acts the other way.
parts.workedSolution: $38\cos 25° = 34.44$ N forwards, so the total along the ground is $34.44 - 15 = 19.44$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: The resolved component is right, so the method mark (M) stands, but a resistance works against the motion and is taken away.
That uses the whole $38$ N. The rope is at an angle, so only $38\cos 25°$ of it acts along the ground.

parts.stem:
A box of mass $16$ kg rests on a ramp inclined at $21°$ to the horizontal.

Calculate the component of the weight of the box acting down the ramp. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Turn the mass into a weight first.
Down the ramp is opposite the ramp's angle.
parts.workedSolution: Weight $= 16 \times 10 = 160$ N, so the component down the ramp is $160\sin 21° = 57.34$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $160\cos 21°$, the component pressing into the ramp. Down the ramp is opposite the ramp's angle, so it takes the sine.
That resolves the mass and swaps the ratio as well. Work out the weight, $160$ N, and take the sine for the component down the ramp.

parts.stem:
Calculate the component of the weight acting at right angles to the ramp. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: Into the ramp sits beside the ramp's angle.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $160\sin 21°$, the component down the ramp. Into the ramp sits beside the ramp's angle, so it takes the cosine.
That is the whole weight. All of it presses into the surface only when the surface is horizontal; on a ramp the cosine takes its share.

parts.stem:
A rope is now attached to the box and pulls it up the ramp. The pull along the rope is $68$ N and the rope makes an angle of $29°$ with the ramp.

Calculate the component of this pull acting along the ramp. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: the angle between the rope and the ramp identified as $29°$

hints: The angle you need is already given, measured from the ramp.
parts.workedSolution: The rope is $29°$ from the ramp, so the component along the ramp is $68\cos 29° = 59.47$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $68\sin 29°$, the component at right angles. The one along the line sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.
That treats the $29°$ as an angle to the horizontal and then works out the angle to the ramp. The question measures it from the ramp already.

questions.solutionProgram: W = 16 * 10; down = W * sin(21 deg); into = W * cos(21 deg); rope = 68 * cos(29 deg)

figures.alt: A ring at O pulled by two forces. A 45 N force acts up and to the right at 38 degrees to the horizontal. A 28 N force acts up and to the left at 55 degrees to the vertical. Dashed horizontal and vertical reference lines cross at O.

parts.stem:
A ring at $O$ is pulled by two ropes. One rope pulls with a force of $45$ N at $38°$ to the horizontal, up and to the right. The other pulls with a force of $28$ N at $55°$ to the vertical, up and to the left.

Calculate the horizontal component of the $45$ N force. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: This angle is measured from the horizontal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $45\sin 38°$, the component at right angles. The one along the line sits beside the angle, so it takes the cosine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the horizontal component of the $28$ N force. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N
hints: This angle is measured from the vertical, so the horizontal is opposite it.
parts.workedSolution: The $55°$ is measured from the vertical, so the horizontal component is $28\sin 55° = 22.94$ N.

commonErrors.feedback: That reads the $55°$ as an angle to the horizontal. It is given to the vertical, so the horizontal component is the one opposite it and takes the sine.

parts.stem:
Calculate the total horizontal component of the two forces, taking the direction to the right as positive. Round to 2 decimal places.

Answer ________ N

scheme.for: both horizontal components used, from (a) and (b)

hints: One component points right, the other left.

commonErrors.feedback: Both components are right, which earns the first method mark (M), but the second force pulls to the left, so its component is subtracted.
That totals the two forces themselves. Only the part of each that lies along the horizontal counts, and one of those parts points the other way.

questions.solutionProgram: h1 = 45 * cos(38 deg); h2 = 28 * sin(55 deg); total = h1 - h2

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara is resolving a force of $30$ N that acts at $50°$ to the vertical. She wants its horizontal component. Her working:
studentWorking: the component along a line is force times cosine of the angle
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 takes the cosine of an angle measured from the vertical, which gives the vertical component, not the horizontal one. The horizontal is at right angles to the vertical, so it is opposite the $50°$ and takes the sine.
correction: the angle is $50°$, measured from the vertical
the horizontal is at right angles to the vertical, so it is opposite the angle
findTheMistake.feedback: Quoting the rule correctly earns the method mark (M). Before choosing sine or cosine, mark the angle on a sketch and ask which side of it the direction you want lies on: beside the angle takes cosine, across from it takes sine.

prompts.prompt: A force $F$ makes an angle $\theta$ with a line. What is its component along that line?
prompts.answer: F cos of theta: the cosine goes with the direction beside the angle.

prompts.prompt: A force $F$ makes an angle $\theta$ with a line. What is its component at right angles to the line?
prompts.answer: F sin of theta, because that direction is opposite the angle.

prompts.prompt: What is the first thing to do before resolving the weight of a body given as a mass?
prompts.answer: Turn the mass into a weight by multiplying by g, which is 10 on this paper.

prompts.prompt: On a slope inclined at an angle to the horizontal, what are the two components of the weight?
prompts.answer: mg sine of the angle down the slope, and mg cosine of the angle into the slope.

prompts.prompt: A force is given at an angle to the vertical. Which ratio gives its horizontal component?
prompts.answer: Sine, because the horizontal is at right angles to the line the angle is measured from.

prompts.prompt: Two components lie along the same line but point opposite ways. How are they combined?
prompts.answer: By subtracting one from the other, since a component has a direction as well as a size.

prompts.prompt: How can the two components of a force be checked once both are worked out?
prompts.answer: Square them, add, and take the square root: the answer comes back to the size of the original force.
